title: A Better Way to Use Criminal Records in Hiring
gist: RAND researchers argue that employer criminal-record screens (felony or violent-offense bans) are about as accurate as a coin toss, while a model using prior convictions, time since last conviction and age predicts reconviction better and is less discriminatory. In a tight labor market, employers using it can reach workers competitors miss.

insights.claim: In a RAND study of about 9.5 million people with convictions across seven states (court and prison records 1992-2021), close to four in five in five states were not reconvicted within the next decade, and two-thirds in Texas and North Carolina.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Blanket no-hire policies exclude a large pool of people who are very likely done offending.
insights.quote: Most of them, it turns out.
insights.locator: For a study published last month

insights.claim: More than half of the people with convictions in the dataset had a five percent or smaller chance of being convicted of anything in the following year.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Individual-level risk is low for most, undermining blanket screening.
insights.locator: The risk is low in the aggregate

insights.claim: Almost a third of American men have an adult conviction, so exclusion rules shrink the available labor pool materially.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Large untapped labor supply for employers facing tight hiring.

insights.claim: Three facts in a criminal record (total prior convictions, time since last conviction, and current age) did nearly all the predictive work for reconviction.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Employers can replace offense-type screens with a simple three-variable model.
insights.locator: Our study found that three simple facts

insights.claim: Offense type adds almost nothing beyond prior count, time since conviction and age, because people who break the law tend to be generalists rather than specialists.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Violent-offense bans, the top employer concern in a RAND survey, are poorly grounded in evidence.

insights.claim: The RAND model scored 0.70 on a scale where 0.50 is a coin flip at one year since the last offense and 0.64 at five years, while felony and violent-offense screens performed substantially worse; after a decade no model predicted well.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: After about ten years, work history and references are better evidence than the record.

insights.claim: Predicting reconviction risk is not the same as predicting job performance, so the hiring manager must still assess reliability and work quality.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: The model is a screen, not a hiring decision.

insights.claim: Employers face a lopsided ledger: a harmful hire risks a rare but costly negligent-hiring suit, while rejecting a safe candidate costs almost nothing when workers are plentiful, though it becomes costly in a tight labor market.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Blanket bans persist from loss aversion; tight labor markets shift the incentives.

insights.claim: Under a 10-year felony threshold, Black men were 74 to 78 percent as likely to be cleared as White women, failing the EEOC 80 percent test, while under the RAND model they were 98 percent as likely.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Chase
insights.so_what: Bright-line screens carry disparate-impact legal exposure that a statistical model reduces.

insights.so_what: Labor-scarce firms gain a hiring edge by dropping blanket record bans.
